set1.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with diabetes took a course of amoxicillin six weeks ago and now has community-acquired pneumonia that will be treated at home with a beta-lactam plus a macrolide. Which beta-lactam fits this outpatient regimen?
opts: Ceftriaxone is the intravenous beta-lactam of the inpatient ward regimen; for outpatient treatment the listed beta-lactams are amoxicillin with or without clavulanic acid, cefuroxime and cefpodoxime.
Cefepime is a fourth-generation antipseudomonal cephalosporin for nosocomial pneumonia with multidrug-resistant risk; outpatient pneumonia pairs cefuroxime or cefpodoxime with a macrolide.
Imipenem/cilastatin is an antipseudomonal carbapenem for broad-spectrum hospital coverage; outpatient pneumonia with resistance risk pairs cefuroxime or cefpodoxime (or amoxicillin) with a macrolide.

Correct. Age over 65, a beta-lactam within the past 3 months and diabetes are risk factors for penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae; outpatients with them get a beta-lactam (amoxicillin with or without clavulanic acid, cefuroxime or cefpodoxime) plus a macrolide.

set1.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 25-year-old woman with allergic asthma is prescribed inhaled cromolyn sodium ahead of a long stay in a home with cats. How should she take it?
opts: At the first sign of wheezing
Cromolyn is not a quick-relief drug; it has to be taken before the antigen insult, and short-acting beta-2 agonists are what treat wheezing.
Taking cromolyn after symptoms start reverses the required timing: it must be taken before the antigen insult and used regularly.
In place of albuterol for attacks
Albuterol is the short-term relief drug; cromolyn is a mast cell stabilizer of limited use that works when taken regularly before exposure.
Correct. Mast cell stabilizers (cromolyn, nedocromil) must be taken before the antigen insult and taken regularly; they may take up to 4 weeks to work.

set1.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 42-year-old woman with asthma develops wheezing every time she takes aspirin. Which oral controller is effective in aspirin-induced asthma?
opts: Cromolyn sodium is an inhaled mast cell stabilizer that must be taken before antigen exposure; the oral controller effective in aspirin-induced asthma is montelukast.

Correct. Montelukast is an oral leukotriene D4 antagonist at the cysteinyl leukotriene 1 receptor (which mediates inflammation, bronchial constriction and mucus secretion) and is effective in aspirin-induced asthma.
Theophylline is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor with a narrow therapeutic index, now of limited use; montelukast is the agent effective in aspirin-induced asthma.
Omalizumab is a subcutaneous anti-immunoglobulin E antibody, not an oral drug; montelukast is the oral agent effective in aspirin-induced asthma.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.topic: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and smoking cessation
set1.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of respiratory drugs
set1.q: A 36-year-old man with a history of depression asks about starting varenicline to quit smoking. Which warning should he be counseled about?
opts: A seizure disorder is a reason to avoid bupropion; varenicline's warning is for neuropsychiatric events such as depression and suicidal ideation.

Correct. Varenicline, a partial nicotine receptor agonist, is listed with a black box warning for neuropsychiatric events (depression, suicidal ideation); its other side effects are nausea, sleep disturbance and headache.
Tachyarrhythmias are the cardiovascular caution for nicotine replacement; varenicline's warning is for neuropsychiatric events such as depression.
Hypertension is nicotine replacement's cardiovascular caution; for varenicline the warning concerns neuropsychiatric events such as depression and suicidal ideation.

set1.topic: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and smoking cessation
set1.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 64-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is breathless only when hurrying or walking up a slight hill and had one exacerbation last year without hospitalization. Which drug treatment is suggested for him?
opts: Correct. Mild or infrequent symptoms with 0 or 1 exacerbation a year and no hospitalization is group A, treated with a short-acting bronchodilator (a beta-2 agonist, a muscarinic antagonist or both) as needed.
Regular long-acting muscarinic antagonist treatment is for group C (high exacerbation risk) or group B; with mild symptoms and low risk, an as-needed short-acting bronchodilator is suggested.
A regular long-acting bronchodilator (beta-2 agonist or muscarinic antagonist) is for the more symptomatic group B; group A gets a short-acting bronchodilator as needed.
An inhaled steroid with a long-acting beta-2 agonist

A combination glucocorticoid and long-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler may be preferred in group D when asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease overlap; group A uses an as-needed short-acting bronchodilator.

set1.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 22-year-old woman's cough from acute bronchitis has lasted more than five days, and testing documents Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Which antibiotic is preferred for her?
opts: Correct. When symptoms persist beyond 5 days, bacterial involvement is considered, and doxycycline is preferred if Mycoplasma is documented because of macrolide resistance.
Azithromycin is a macrolide; macrolides are listed for persistent bronchitis, but documented Mycoplasma calls for doxycycline because of macrolide resistance.
Levofloxacin is a respiratory fluoroquinolone, avoided in bronchitis unless there was recent antibiotic exposure (risk of resistant pneumococcus); doxycycline is preferred for Mycoplasma.
ruled out by a stated finding
Cefuroxime is a cephalosporin paired with a macrolide for community-acquired pneumonia with resistance risk; it is not on the bronchitis list, where doxycycline is preferred for Mycoplasma.

set1.topic: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and smoking cessation
set1.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 41-year-old woman sets a quit date three weeks from now and is prescribed varenicline. When should she start taking it?
opts: On the morning of her quit date
Varenicline is not started on the quit date itself; it is begun one week before the quit date and continued for 12 weeks.
Starting after quitting reverses the timing; varenicline begins one week before the quit date and continues for 12 weeks.
One week before her quit date
Correct. Varenicline, a partial nicotine receptor agonist, is started one week before the quit date and continued for 12 weeks.
Varenicline is not taken on demand for cravings; it is started one week before the quit date and continued for 12 weeks.

set1.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 78-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease cannot generate a strong, deep inhalation. Which device should be avoided for him?
opts: Correct. A dry powder inhaler relies on the patient's own inspiratory force to draw the powder out of the device, so it is not good for patients with poor inspiratory capacity.
A nebulizer's compressor makes a mist for passive inhalation, which suits patients who cannot use other devices; the device to avoid with weak inspiration is a dry powder inhaler.
ruled out by a stated finding
Metered dose inhaler with a spacer
In a metered dose inhaler a propellant forces the medicine out, and a spacer holds it for patients with poor coordination; weak inspiratory force rules out the dry powder inhaler instead.
ruled out by a stated finding
Inhaler with a valve holding chamber
A valve holding chamber has one-way valves and holds the inhaler's mist; the device that depends on a strong inhalation is the dry powder inhaler.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Discuss potential drug-drug, drug-food, and drug-herb interactions with drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 26-year-old woman starting four-drug therapy for active pulmonary tuberculosis takes an oral contraceptive. Which drug in her regimen can make the contraceptive less reliable?
opts: Isoniazid's listed problems are hepatitis, peripheral neuritis, a lupus-like reaction and central nervous system effects; the enzyme inducer that affects contraceptives is rifampin.
Correct. Rifampin induces cytochrome P450 enzymes, and contraceptives and anticoagulants are among the drugs it affects.
Ethambutol's adverse effects are visual disturbances and raised uric acid, and it is mostly excreted unchanged; rifampin is the enzyme inducer that affects contraceptives.
Pyrazinamide's concerns are hepatitis and hyperuricemia, and it is avoided in pregnancy; the cytochrome P450 inducer that affects contraceptives is rifampin.

set1.io: Describe adverse effects of drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 45-year-old man taking isoniazid for tuberculosis develops numbness and tingling in his feet. Which vitamin should be given?
opts: Thiamine is not the deficiency behind isoniazid's peripheral neuritis; that neuritis comes from pyridoxine deficiency, and pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is given.
Folic acid does not correct isoniazid's peripheral neuritis, which comes from pyridoxine deficiency; pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is the vitamin to give.
Correct. Isoniazid causes peripheral neuritis through pyridoxine deficiency, so pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is given.
Cobalamin deficiency is not the mechanism of isoniazid neuritis; isoniazid causes pyridoxine deficiency, so pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is given.

set1.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with asthma cannot time pressing her metered dose inhaler with breathing in, but she wants to keep using it. Which addition helps her?
opts: Pressing two puffs back to back
Puffs of a quick-relief inhaler are separated by 15 to 30 seconds, not pressed back to back; poor coordination is helped by a spacer, which holds the medication.
She should breathe out all the way before the puff, not into the device (a valve holding chamber's valves block exhaling into it); a spacer helps the timing problem.
The breath is held for 10 seconds or as long as comfortable after inhaling; skipping it is not the fix for poor coordination, which a spacer addresses.
A spacer to hold the puff
Correct. A metered dose inhaler requires the most coordination of the devices, and spacers are used to hold the medication for patients with poor coordination.

set1.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of respiratory drugs
set1.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease uses tiotropium, inhaled fluticasone, albuterol as needed and theophylline. He develops nausea, vomiting and palpitations, then has a seizure. Which drug most likely caused this?
opts: Tiotropium's anticholinergic effects are blurry vision, flushing, fever, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and tachycardia; nausea with a seizure points to theophylline.
Inhaled fluticasone causes oral thrush, growth suppression in children and immune inhibition; nausea, palpitations and a seizure point to theophylline toxicity.
Correct. Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index; nausea, vomiting and cardiac effects appear first, then seizures and arrhythmias as levels climb, which is why its plasma levels are monitored.
Albuterol can cause tachycardia, tremor and headache, but seizures are not on its list; theophylline causes nausea, vomiting, arrhythmias and convulsions.

set1.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 59-year-old man receiving mechanical ventilation develops pneumonia on hospital day 8. He is started on cefepime plus tobramycin. Which drug must be added?
opts: Azithromycin is a macrolide for community-acquired pneumonia; the missing piece of this broad nosocomial regimen is gram-positive coverage with vancomycin or linezolid.

Ciprofloxacin is an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone that can serve as the second gram-negative agent, but tobramycin already fills that role; gram-positive coverage with vancomycin or linezolid is missing.
Ertapenem is a narrow-spectrum carbapenem with limited activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, used for limited-spectrum coverage; this regimen still lacks vancomycin or linezolid.

Correct. Late onset (5 days or more) calls for broad-spectrum therapy for multidrug-resistant pathogens: gram-negative combination therapy (cefepime plus an aminoglycoside here) plus gram-positive coverage with vancomycin or linezolid, since methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas must both be covered.

set1.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 72-year-old man who received intravenous antibiotics last month develops ventilator-associated pneumonia on hospital day 6. Which empiric regimen is appropriate?
opts: Meropenem and piperacillin-tazobactam are both antipseudomonal beta-lactams; the second gram-negative agent must be an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone or an aminoglycoside.

Correct. Risk factors for multidrug-resistant pathogens call for broad coverage: an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam) plus an aminoglycoside (tobramycin) plus gram-positive coverage (linezolid).
Vancomycin and linezolid both cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, so only levofloxacin covers gram-negative organisms; broad coverage needs two.
ruled out by a stated finding
Ceftriaxone with a macrolide treats community-acquired pneumonia; neither is antipseudomonal, so the gram-negative combination for this patient is missing.

set1.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of respiratory drugs
set1.q: A 38-year-old man with severe allergic asthma receives his first subcutaneous omalizumab injection. Which serious adverse effect is listed for this drug?
opts: Oral candidiasis (thrush) comes from inhaled corticosteroids; omalizumab is injected, and its serious listed adverse effect is anaphylaxis.
Seizures (convulsions) are a theophylline toxicity at high levels; the serious listed adverse effect of omalizumab is anaphylaxis.

Correct. Omalizumab's listed adverse effects include anaphylaxis (about 0.1%), urticaria, gastrointestinal disturbances, injection site pain, bruising, neutralizing antibodies and secondary malignancies.
Tremor is a beta-2 agonist adverse effect; the serious listed adverse effect of omalizumab, an anti-immunoglobulin E antibody, is anaphylaxis.

set1.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of respiratory drugs
set1.q: A 40-year-old woman six weeks into four-drug tuberculosis therapy says traffic-light colors look washed out and she struggles to tell red from green. Which drug is responsible?
opts: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuritis (from pyridoxine deficiency), hepatitis and central nervous system effects; red-green color loss is ethambutol's.
Rifampin colors tears, sweat and urine orange and induces cytochrome P450 enzymes; loss of red-green discrimination is ethambutol's visual toxicity.
Correct. Ethambutol's adverse effects include visual disturbances: decreased red-green discrimination and decreased visual acuity.
Pyrazinamide causes hepatitis and hyperuricemia; decreased red-green discrimination and visual acuity belong to ethambutol.

set1.io: Describe absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 67-year-old woman with worsening kidney function has late-onset hospital-acquired pneumonia and needs coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which drug needs no dose adjustment for her kidney function?
opts: Vancomycin covers methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus but requires renal adjustment and is nephrotoxic with other nephrotoxins; linezolid needs no renal dose adjustment.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Linezolid gives great methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage with good lung penetration, comes in intravenous and oral forms, and needs no dose adjustment based on renal function.
Tobramycin is an aminoglycoside whose dosing is highly dependent on renal function (ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity), and it is gram-negative coverage; linezolid needs no renal adjustment.
ruled out by a stated finding
Cefepime is an antipseudomonal cephalosporin that requires renal adjustment and does not cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus; linezolid needs no renal adjustment.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 19-year-old woman stung by a bee develops hives, wheezing, throat tightness and low blood pressure. She is conscious and has a pulse. Which treatment acts on both her blood pressure and her airways?
opts: Intravenous crystalloids (sodium chloride) increase intravascular volume for profound vasodilation and hypotension, but they have no listed effect on the airways; epinephrine acts on both.
Diphenhydramine is a histamine H1 blocker that relieves rash, itching and hives (the cutaneous effects); epinephrine is the drug acting on both blood vessels and airways.
Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle but does not cause vasoconstriction; epinephrine acts on both alpha and beta receptors.

Correct. Epinephrine acts on alpha receptors (vasoconstriction, decreased vascular permeability) and beta receptors (bronchial smooth muscle relaxation), and intramuscular injection is preferred unless the patient is coding.

set1.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 34-year-old man has had a cough, low-grade fever and chest soreness for three days, starting after a cold. He is diagnosed with acute bronchitis and is otherwise well. Which approach is recommended?
opts: Correct. Acute bronchitis is usually viral (rhinovirus, coronavirus, influenza, adenovirus) and generally self-limited, so care is symptomatic and supportive (analgesics, antipyretics, antitussives, fluids); routine antibiotics are not recommended.
Antibiotics are considered only when symptoms persist beyond 5 days and bacteria may be involved; at three days, routine antibiotics are not recommended and care is supportive.
Doxycycline is preferred once Mycoplasma is documented, because of macrolide resistance; nothing documents it here, so supportive care without an antibiotic is the approach.
ruled out by a stated finding
A respiratory fluoroquinolone is avoided unless there was recent antibiotic exposure, because of the risk of resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae; this self-limited illness needs supportive care.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 62-year-old man develops anaphylaxis minutes after receiving an antibiotic, becomes pulseless, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation begins. By which route should his epinephrine now be given?
opts: Intramuscular injection is the usual preferred route, but not for a patient who is coding; with cardiopulmonary resuscitation underway, epinephrine goes intravenously.

Correct. Epinephrine can be given intramuscularly, subcutaneously or intravenously; intramuscular is generally preferred unless the patient is coding, as he now is, and in cardiac arrest the standard route is intravenous (resuscitation practice).

Subcutaneous injection is a listed route, but once a patient is coding the intramuscular preference ends, leaving intravenous or subcutaneous; in cardiac arrest the standard route is intravenous (resuscitation practice).
Inhalation is not a listed route for epinephrine in anaphylaxis; it is given intramuscularly, subcutaneously or intravenously, and in cardiac arrest the standard route is intravenous.

set1.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set1.q: A 50-year-old man with active pulmonary tuberculosis asks why he must take several drugs instead of one. What is the main reason?
opts: Correct. Single agents are not used in active disease, to prevent the development of resistance; rifampin is rarely used alone because of rapid tolerance, and ethambutol resistance develops quickly if it is used alone.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows very slowly and can lie dormant for long periods; the reason for several drugs in active disease is to prevent resistance.
To lower the risk of liver damage
Liver toxicity is the reason pyrazinamide is limited to the first two months, not the reason for combining drugs; several drugs are used to prevent resistance.
To allow a lower dose of each drug
Combination therapy is not about smaller doses; single agents are avoided in active disease to prevent the development of resistance.

set2.io: Describe adverse effects of drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 35-year-old woman started inhaled fluticasone a month ago and now has white plaques on her tongue and inner cheeks. Which adverse effect is this?
opts: Dry mouth is an anticholinergic effect (dry as a bone) of ipratropium and tiotropium; white oral plaques on an inhaled corticosteroid are thrush.
Correct. Oral candidiasis (thrush) is a listed adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroids, along with growth suppression in children at high doses and inhibition of the immune system.
Angioedema is part of anaphylaxis and is relieved by epinephrine; white plaques on the tongue and cheeks after starting an inhaled corticosteroid are thrush.
Neutralizing antibodies may develop with omalizumab, an injected anti-immunoglobulin E antibody; fluticasone's oral adverse effect is candidiasis (thrush).

set2.topic: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and smoking cessation
set2.io: Identify contraindications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 45-year-old man with a seizure disorder wants medication to help him quit smoking. Which agent should be avoided?
opts: Varenicline's listed effects are nausea, sleep disturbance, headache and a neuropsychiatric warning, with no seizure contraindication listed; bupropion is avoided in seizure disorders.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Bupropion (sustained release, Zyban) is to be avoided in patients with seizure disorders and in patients taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors.
Nicotine patches call for caution in cardiovascular problems (tachyarrhythmias, hypertension), not in seizure disorders; bupropion is the agent to avoid.
ruled out by a stated finding
Nicotine gum (nicotine polacrilex), like the patch, is cautioned for cardiovascular problems; the smoking cessation agent avoided in seizure disorders is bupropion.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 64-year-old woman develops pneumonia on hospital day 3 after hip surgery. She has had no antibiotics or hospital stays in the past 90 days, no known colonization with resistant organisms, does not live in a care facility and is not immunosuppressed. Which drug is a limited-spectrum empiric choice for her?
opts: Cefepime is an antipseudomonal cephalosporin, part of broad-spectrum combination therapy for patients with multidrug-resistant risk factors, which she does not have.

Vancomycin is the gram-positive (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) arm of broad-spectrum coverage for multidrug-resistant risk; she qualifies for limited-spectrum therapy such as ceftriaxone.
Piperacillin/tazobactam is an antipseudomonal penicillin used in broad-spectrum gram-negative combination therapy; without multidrug-resistant risk factors, limited-spectrum ceftriaxone fits.

Correct. Early onset (before day 5) with no risk factors for multidrug-resistant pathogens calls for limited-spectrum therapy: ceftriaxone, or levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, or ampicillin/sulbactam, or ertapenem.

set2.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 32-year-old woman in status asthmaticus is intubated after continuous nebulized albuterol, intravenous steroids and magnesium have failed. Which drug may be added now that she is intubated?
opts: Correct. Ketamine is used in status asthmaticus once the patient is intubated: a dissociative anesthetic (N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist) that increases catecholamine release and causes bronchodilation.
Salmeterol is a long-acting beta-2 agonist controller that is not used alone for asthma and is not part of the status asthmaticus algorithm; ketamine is added if intubated.
Cromolyn sodium is a preventive mast cell stabilizer that must be taken before an antigen insult; the status asthmaticus algorithm adds ketamine once she is intubated.
Omalizumab is a subcutaneous anti-immunoglobulin E antibody for long-term control; the status asthmaticus algorithm adds ketamine when the patient is intubated.

set2.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 45-year-old woman's asthma stays uncontrolled on high-dose inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta-2 agonist, despite good inhaler technique and adherence. Her peripheral blood eosinophils are 400 per microliter. Which add-on drug fits her phenotype?
opts: Cromolyn sodium is a mast cell stabilizer of limited use that must be taken before antigen exposure; the eosinophilic phenotype is treated with a biologic such as mepolizumab.

Correct. The anti-interleukin-5 biologics (mepolizumab, benralizumab, reslizumab) and the anti-interleukin-4 drug dupilumab are used for the eosinophilic phenotype (peripheral blood eosinophils above 150 per microliter).
Theophylline is a nonspecific phosphodiesterase inhibitor that is less effective and less well tolerated than long-acting bronchodilators; mepolizumab is the eosinophil-directed biologic.
Ipratropium is a short-acting anticholinergic quick-relief drug; an eosinophilic phenotype calls for a biologic such as mepolizumab.

set2.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 35-year-old woman being treated for anaphylaxis has received epinephrine and diphenhydramine, and famotidine is added. Which effects does famotidine block?
opts: Rash, pruritus and hives are the cutaneous effects relieved by histamine H1 blockers such as diphenhydramine and hydroxyzine, not by the H2 blocker famotidine.
Bronchial smooth muscle relaxation comes from beta stimulation by epinephrine or albuterol; famotidine blocks histamine's vasodilation and gastric effects.
Correct. Famotidine is a histamine H2 blocker: it blocks the systemic effects (vasodilation) and gastrointestinal effects (increased gastric acid secretion) of the massive histamine release.
Blocking the production of inflammatory mediators at the cellular level is the corticosteroid action (methylprednisolone, prednisone); famotidine blocks histamine at H2 receptors.

set2.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 4-year-old girl with asthma will use a nebulizer at home because she cannot use a metered dose inhaler. What should her parents be told about the nebulizer?
opts: It needs a strong, fast inhalation
A strong inspiratory effort is what a dry powder inhaler needs; a nebulizer's compressor makes a fine mist for passive inhalation.
Coordinating the press with the breath is the demand of a metered dose inhaler; a nebulizer allows passive inhalation.
It gives a bigger dose, so more side effects

Correct. A nebulizer allows passive inhalation, which suits children and older adults who cannot use a metered dose inhaler, but it delivers a bigger dose overall and may lead to more side effects; it must also be cleaned regularly.
It can go without regular cleaning
A nebulizer must be cleaned regularly to prevent microbial growth; its other drawback is a bigger overall dose with more side effects.

set2.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 70-year-old man with ventilator-associated pneumonia receives tobramycin as part of broad-spectrum coverage. Which pair of toxicities should his monitoring target?
opts: Correct. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; dose and frequency are adjusted on drug levels and depend heavily on renal function.
Hepatitis and hyperuricemia are pyrazinamide's adverse effects in tuberculosis therapy; aminoglycosides are monitored for ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.
Decreased red-green discrimination and visual acuity are ethambutol's adverse effects; tobramycin's are ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity, tracked with drug levels and renal function.
Tachycardia and hyperglycemia are beta-2 agonist adverse effects; an aminoglycoside such as tobramycin is monitored for ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.

set2.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 30-year-old man with no medical problems has community-acquired pneumonia and will be treated at home. He has no risk factors for drug-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae. Which drug is first line?
opts: Doxycycline is the second-line outpatient choice when there is no resistance risk; the first-line choice is a macrolide such as azithromycin.

A respiratory fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin is for outpatients with risk factors for resistant pneumococcus or a beta-lactam allergy; he has no resistance risk factors, so a macrolide is first line.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. With no risk of resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, outpatient first-line therapy is a macrolide (azithromycin or clarithromycin); doxycycline or minocycline is second line.
Cefpodoxime is the beta-lactam partner of a macrolide for patients with resistance risk factors; without such risk, a macrolide such as azithromycin is first line.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Identify contraindications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 48-year-old man with a seizure disorder develops late-onset hospital-acquired pneumonia, and the team wants an antipseudomonal carbapenem. Which drug is the better choice for him?
opts: Imipenem/cilastatin is an antipseudomonal carbapenem but is used with caution in patients with a seizure history; meropenem carries less seizure risk.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Imipenem/cilastatin is used with caution in patients with a seizure history, while meropenem carries less risk for seizures; both are antipseudomonal carbapenems that require renal adjustment.
Ertapenem is a narrow-spectrum carbapenem with limited activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, so it does not give the antipseudomonal coverage he needs; meropenem does.
ruled out by a stated finding
Cefepime is a fourth-generation antipseudomonal cephalosporin, not a carbapenem; among the carbapenems, meropenem carries less seizure risk than imipenem/cilastatin.

set2.io: Identify contraindications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 27-year-old woman who is 12 weeks pregnant is diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which first-line drug should be avoided?
opts: Isoniazid's cautions are hepatitis (more with alcohol and with age) and neuritis needing pyridoxine; avoidance in pregnancy is listed for pyrazinamide.
Rifampin's concerns are enzyme induction, hepatitis, orange secretions and a flu-like syndrome; the first-line drug listed to avoid in pregnancy is pyrazinamide.
Correct. Pyrazinamide is to be avoided in pregnancy; it also causes hepatitis (monitor liver enzymes) and makes patients hyperuricemic.
Ethambutol's adverse effects are visual disturbances and raised uric acid; the first-line drug to avoid in pregnancy is pyrazinamide.

set2.topic: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and smoking cessation
set2.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 70-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has mild symptoms but had two exacerbations last year, one needing hospitalization. Which regular treatment is suggested?
opts: Correct. Mild symptoms with 2 or more exacerbations a year (one or more hospitalized) is group C: regular long-acting muscarinic antagonist treatment, with a short-acting beta-2 agonist for symptom relief as needed.
As-needed short-acting bronchodilators are group A treatment (low risk); her two exacerbations with a hospitalization put her in group C, treated with a regular long-acting muscarinic antagonist.
A regular long-acting beta-2 agonist is one choice for group B (more symptoms, low risk); for group C the suggested regular treatment is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist.
An inhaled steroid with a long-acting beta-2 agonist
A combination glucocorticoid and long-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler may be preferred in group D when features of asthma overlap; group C gets a regular long-acting muscarinic antagonist.

set2.io: Describe adverse effects of drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 58-year-old man who drinks heavily is starting isoniazid for tuberculosis. Which adverse effect is more likely because of his drinking?
opts: Correct. Isoniazid hepatitis increases in alcoholics and with age, so liver injury is the risk his drinking raises.
A lupus-like syndrome is isoniazid's allergic reaction, not one linked to alcohol; the adverse effect that increases in alcoholics is hepatitis.
Loss of red-green discrimination is an ethambutol visual disturbance, not an isoniazid effect; isoniazid's alcohol-linked risk is hepatitis.
Orange-colored tears, sweat and urine come from rifampin, not isoniazid; with isoniazid, alcoholism increases the risk of hepatitis.

set2.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 24-year-old woman with asthma now uses her albuterol inhaler several times a day and wakes most nights coughing. What does this pattern of albuterol use call for?
opts: Levalbuterol is another short-acting beta-2 agonist; excessive reliever use signals poor control, which calls for adjusting long-term controller therapy.
Albuterol remains her quick-relief medicine; what excessive use indicates is poor control and the need to adjust her long-term controller therapy.
Long-acting beta-2 agonists such as salmeterol are not to be used alone for asthma; poor control calls for adjusting long-term controller therapy.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Albuterol provides only short-term relief and should be used sparingly; excessive use indicates poor control and the need to adjust long-term controller therapy.

set2.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman is admitted to a hospital ward with community-acquired pneumonia. Before her first antibiotic dose, which step is recommended?
opts: Skipping diagnostic tests is the outpatient approach, where patients do well with empiric antibiotics; hospitalized patients have blood and sputum cultures drawn before antibiotics.
Correct. For hospitalized patients, blood and sputum cultures are obtained before antibiotics are given; outpatients, by contrast, do well with empiric antibiotics and are not routinely tested.
Rely on a sputum Gram stain alone
Sputum Gram stain and culture are controversial: expectorated sputum is often contaminated and the pathogen is not always identified; blood and sputum cultures are drawn before antibiotics.
The order is reversed: for hospitalized patients, blood and sputum cultures are to be drawn before the first antibiotic dose is given.

set2.topic: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and smoking cessation
set2.io: Identify contraindications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 58-year-old man with coronary artery disease plans to quit smoking with nicotine patches. Which risk calls for caution in him?
opts: Seizure disorders are a reason to avoid bupropion, not a listed nicotine caution; nicotine's caution in heart disease is tachyarrhythmias and hypertension.
Depression and suicidal ideation are the neuropsychiatric events in varenicline's warning; nicotine replacement's caution is tachyarrhythmias and hypertension.
Correct. Nicotine replacement calls for caution in patients with cardiovascular problems because of the chance of tachyarrhythmias and hypertension.
Nausea, sleep disturbance and headache are varenicline's listed side effects; in a patient with heart disease, nicotine's caution is tachyarrhythmias and hypertension.

set2.topic: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and smoking cessation
set2.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease asks which vaccines she should receive. Which recommendation fits her?
opts: Influenza vaccination is recommended every year, not just in outbreak years, and the pneumococcal vaccine is added; the recommendation is annual influenza plus pneumococcal.
The pneumococcal vaccine is given in addition to, not instead of, the annual influenza vaccine; both are recommended in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
No vaccines until her disease is stable
Waiting is not the advice: annual influenza vaccination is highly recommended in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and the pneumococcal vaccine should also be given.

Correct. Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are at risk of serious illness and death from pneumonia caused by influenza; annual influenza vaccination is highly recommended, and they should also receive the pneumococcal vaccine.

set2.io: Identify contraindications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 28-year-old man with persistent asthma asks to use salmeterol by itself as his one controller medicine. What should he be told?
opts: It must be paired with an inhaled steroid
Correct. Long-acting beta-2 agonists (formoterol, salmeterol) are not to be used alone for asthma; they are combined with an inhaled corticosteroid, as in salmeterol/fluticasone (Advair).
It can replace albuterol during attacks
Salmeterol is a long-acting controller lasting 12 hours or more, not a quick-relief drug; short-acting albuterol relieves attacks, and salmeterol is not used alone for asthma.
It is safe alone if taken twice daily
Long-acting beta-2 agonists are not to be used alone for asthma, however they are scheduled; salmeterol must be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid.
It treats the airway inflammation itself
Salmeterol relaxes airway smooth muscle by raising cyclic adenosine monophosphate; controlling inflammation is the job of inhaled corticosteroids, which it must be paired with.

set2.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 30-year-old woman has latent tuberculosis infection with no sign of active disease. Which drug is the one used by itself for prophylaxis?
opts: Resistance to ethambutol develops quickly if it is used alone; it belongs to combination therapy for active disease, while isoniazid alone is the prophylactic drug.
Pyrazinamide is given in the first two months of combination therapy for active disease, where it shortens treatment; prophylaxis uses isoniazid alone.
Doxycycline is a second-line outpatient choice for community-acquired pneumonia without resistance risk; isoniazid used alone is the listed prophylactic drug.
Correct. Isoniazid is used alone for prophylaxis and in combination therapy for active disease; it is bacteriostatic for latent and bactericidal for dividing bacteria.

set2.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 72-year-old man with heart failure has community-acquired pneumonia that will be treated at home. He had hives and throat swelling after penicillin. Which drug covers his resistance risk without a beta-lactam?
opts: Correct. With risk factors for resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae (age over 65, heart failure), a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin) can replace a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, and it is good for patients with a beta-lactam allergy.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a beta-lactam, which his penicillin reaction argues against; a respiratory fluoroquinolone is the listed choice for a beta-lactam allergy.
ruled out by a stated finding
Cefuroxime is a second-generation cephalosporin, a beta-lactam paired with a macrolide; with a beta-lactam allergy, a respiratory fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin is the choice.
ruled out by a stated finding
Azithromycin by itself suits outpatients without resistance risk; his age over 65 and heart failure call for a respiratory fluoroquinolone or a beta-lactam plus a macrolide.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
set2.q: A 45-year-old man has finished the first two months of four-drug therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis. Which drugs continue for the next four months?
opts: Ethambutol belongs to the first two months of four-drug therapy; the four-month continuation is isoniazid with rifampin.
Pyrazinamide is given in the first two months only, to avoid liver toxicity; the four-month continuation is isoniazid with rifampin.
Ethambutol and pyrazinamide both belong to the two-month four-drug phase; isoniazid and rifampin are the two drugs continued for four more months.
Correct. Combination therapy is isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide for 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months.
